The phase case
Jordan returns to the next free throw
Jordan is a fictional Grade 10 basketball player. During open play, Jordan needs to notice the ball,
defenders and available teammates. At the free-throw line, the task changes. Jordan has practised a
brief setup: find the line, release extra shoulder tension, look at the chosen rim target and use the
cue “smooth.”
At the last school practice, Jordan missed a shot after a rushed setup. Jordan then thought, “I
always fail when people watch,” looked toward a spectator and missed the teammate's signal for the
next drill. The coach observed the rushed setup and offered a chance to practise it again. One
missed cue does not tell us its only cause. In this case, Jordan's own account supplies additional
evidence about attention.
The next practice includes a planned interruption: the drill order changes before Jordan's turn. You
will help Jordan prepare, notice the new demand and select a useful next cue. Treat the case as
fictional. An academic parallel is preparing to explain a graph after a classroom presentation order
changes. An artistic parallel is returning to an agreed musical entry after an interruption. You may
use one of these settings throughout your work.
Your opening response
Describe Jordan’s task before a free throw and during open play. What useful information changes
between those moments?
Learning goals
I can explain selection, sustaining attention and shifting using a specific task.
I can distinguish the four attention quadrants in a clearly stated moment.
I can explain a sequence of attention shifts and the trigger for each change.
I can use an attributed coaching framework without treating it as a measured equation.
I can select a cue and anchor that fit a particular task.
I can explain the purpose of each step in a before-performance routine.
I can write an adaptable if–then plan that returns attention to useful information.
I can propose a suitable variation and explain what evidence would guide an adjustment.

chunks.text:
Learning goal: I can explain selection, sustaining attention and shifting using a specific task.
Before you begin: Picture a performer who has more information available than they can use
at once.
Attention gives the task a place to start
A school gym contains voices, moving people, floor markings and a scoreboard. A player cannot
treat every detail as equally important. Attention concerns how information is selected and used.
Concentration means keeping attention with what matters for the task. It does not mean blocking
out everything around you.
Four useful actions are selecting, sustaining, noticing and shifting. Selecting means choosing
information. Sustaining means staying with it long enough to do the job. Noticing means detecting
a relevant change. Shifting means moving attention when another cue becomes more useful.
These actions often work together rather than appearing as four separate stages.
Select according to the demand
Ask, “What decision or action is needed now?” A player deciding where to pass needs different
information from a player taking a free throw. A presenter explaining a graph needs to attend to its
key relationship. Reading every word on a slide may compete with that job.
Useful information is task-relevant: it helps the current action. A distraction pulls attention toward
something less useful at that moment. The same sound can serve either role. A musician may need
a partner's entry cue, while an unrelated conversation adds nothing to the next phrase. Relevance
depends on the task, not just whether the information is inside or outside the performer.
Capacity is limited
Trying to hold many instructions at once can make the next action unclear. “Watch everyone,
remember every correction and never make a mistake” gives attention several competing jobs. A
shorter cue can help organize a familiar action. It cannot supply a skill the person has not learned.
Limited capacity does not mean a person is unable to learn. It means the plan should decide what
deserves attention now. During learning, there may be time to examine a movement carefully.
During a familiar performance, one well-understood cue may be more usable than a list of
corrections.
Notice before explaining a miss
A missed cue is an observation. Its cause is a further question. The cue might have been unclear,
unexpected or hidden. The performer might have been attending elsewhere. Ask what was noticed,
what the person was trying to do and whether the instructions changed.

A useful plan does not demand perfect concentration. It identifies the relevant information, provides
a way to notice drift and names a return point. The next topics give more precise language for that
plan.
Worked example · fictional case
One room, two different jobs
Mina is preparing a short class presentation. Before speaking, Mina checks the graph's main
relationship. During the explanation, Mina notices a classmate's question. Looking at the
graph was useful first; listening becomes useful next.
A phone notification is less relevant to either task. The plan is to silence it during preparation,
then use “main relationship” as the opening cue. This supports selection and sustaining
attention. It does not mean Mina must ignore a relevant question to prove concentration.

03 · Four ways to focus
Describe attention by its width and its direction.
Learning goal: I can distinguish the four attention quadrants in a clearly stated moment.
Before you begin: Separate how much information is used from where that information
comes from.
Two questions form four quadrants
The attention framework associated with Robert Nideffer combines two dimensions. Width
describes whether attention is broad or narrow. Direction describes whether it is internal or external.
Broad attention takes in several pieces of information. Narrow attention selects a specific cue.
Internal attention concerns thoughts or bodily sensations. External attention concerns information in
the surroundings.
Combine the dimensions to name four quadrants: broad-external, broad-internal, narrow-internal
and narrow-external. These labels describe the focus used in a moment. They do not divide
students into permanent kinds of people. A useful performer can change focus when the demand
changes.
Broad-external: scan the surroundings
A basketball player scans the ball, defenders and available teammates before a pass. Several
external cues matter together. That is a broad-external example. Broad does not mean noticing
everything equally. It means gathering enough relevant information to read the play.
A recreational hiker checking the route, group position and nearby conditions offers another
example. The situation determines which details belong in the scan. Looking around without a
purpose may simply add distractions.

chunks.text:
Broad-internal: consider information and options
During a pause, a player considers the coach's plan, the available options and an earlier pattern in
the game. Those thoughts are internal, and several pieces are being considered. This is broad-
internal attention.
A student organizing the argument for a presentation also uses several internal ideas. Analysis can
be useful when there is time for it. The question is whether the current moment calls for planning or
for carrying out the next prepared action.
Narrow-internal: one thought or sensation
During a safe pause, a performer briefly checks whether their shoulders are unnecessarily tense.
The focus is internal and specific. Recalling one short cue can also be narrow-internal. This is
different from repeatedly scanning every possible bodily sensation.
An internal check should have a clear purpose and an ending. After the check, the performer returns
to information needed for the task. A long search for a perfect feeling may compete with preparation.
Narrow-external: one useful outside cue
A free-throw shooter looks at a chosen part of the rim. A musician watches the conductor's entry
signal. Each selects a specific external cue. Narrow attention is useful here because the next action
has a precise target.
No quadrant is always best. A narrow target that helps a free throw may hide useful information
during open play. Judge the focus against the task rather than calling broad, narrow, internal or
external attention automatically good or bad.
Worked example · fictional case
Describe the moment, not the whole athlete
Jordan is waiting at the free-throw line. During a safe pause, Jordan briefly notices extra
shoulder tension. This is narrow-internal attention: one bodily cue. Jordan then looks at the
chosen rim target, which is narrow-external.
The framework describes two moments in the same routine. It does not prove that Jordan
belongs to an “internal type.” Once play resumes, a wider scan may be needed. The
explanation must include the task and timing of each focus.

chunks.titleGuess: NEXT STEP · SPORTS PSYCHOLOGY Phase 3 — The Focus

chunks.text:
A useful focus can become an old focus
During open play, Jordan scans defenders and teammates. A whistle stops the play. The coach
gives a short instruction. Later, Jordan takes a free throw. Holding exactly the same focus across
these moments would not meet all three demands.
An   attention shift is a change in the information selected. It may change width, direction or both. A
plan is stronger when it names what triggers the shift. “Focus better” is vague. “When the whistle
stops play, listen for the instruction” links an event to a useful response.
Scan, plan, check and target
One teaching sequence begins with a broad-external scan of the situation. During a suitable pause,
broad-internal attention may help the performer consider options. A brief narrow-internal check may
identify an unnecessary tension signal. Narrow-external attention can then select the target for a
precise next action.
This sequence is an example, not a ritual everyone must complete. Some tasks need fewer shifts.
Others require repeated scanning during action. The performer should not add an internal check if it
distracts from information needed for safety or execution. The task decides the sequence.
Give every transition a reason
For each moment, name the demand, the information and the trigger. A passing decision calls for
information about space and teammates. A planned break permits discussion. An aiming attempt
calls for the established target. The transition matters because the information needs have changed.
A musician may listen broadly to the ensemble, consider an adjustment during a pause, briefly recall
the agreed count and then watch a specific entry cue. A presenter may scan the audience for a
question, think through a response, choose the relevant example and point to one part of a graph.
Neither situation needs a sport setting to use the framework.
Avoid two common traps
The first trap is staying with the last mistake. The result has happened, but attention remains on a
judgment instead of the next demand. A brief factual review can be useful later. During the next
action, use a cue that belongs to that action.
The second trap is changing focus without a reason. Constantly checking body sensations, the
score and other people's reactions can create competing jobs. A prepared transition can reduce
unnecessary searching, while remaining flexible when new information matters.

chunks.text:
Check whether the shift served the task
Record what the performer intended to notice and what they actually noticed. Did the cue make the
next action clearer? Was important information missed? One result does not prove that the shift
caused success or failure. Use the observation to decide what to keep, clarify or practise again.
Worked example · fictional case
The whistle changes the job
Jordan scans the ball and available teammates during play. When the whistle sounds, the
task becomes listening to the official rather than continuing the pass. At the free-throw line,
Jordan uses the familiar setup and chosen target.
A useful plan names those transitions. It does not instruct Jordan to repeat all four quadrants
while the ball is live. Attention shifts because the task changes, not because completing a
four-box sequence earns a better result.

chunks.text:
A mistake and its interpretation are different
“The ball landed short” describes a result. “I am useless” judges the whole person. The second
statement gives little direction for the next attempt. It may also compete with information the
performer needs. A useful response starts with what happened and what can be examined.
Nonjudgmental observation means describing a relevant feature without turning it into a verdict on
personal worth. It does not mean pretending the attempt was correct. A performer can acknowledge
a missed shot and ask for feedback without calling themselves a failure.
Gallwey's Inner Game framework
Timothy Gallwey uses the coaching framework performance = potential − interference. Here,
interference means influences that get in the way of using a learned skill. Excessive self-criticism or
trying to control every small movement may be examples in a particular case.
Treat the equation as an organizing idea, not arithmetic. This lesson does not measure a student's
potential or subtract a numerical amount of interference. Many other features of a task matter,
including instruction, preparation, skill and conditions.
The framework uses Self 1 for the telling, judging voice and Self 2 for the performer using learned
capabilities. These are model labels. They are not two brain structures or two separate people inside
a learner. Their purpose is to help discuss how commentary can compete with execution.
Analysis still has a place
A beginner may need a demonstration and careful attention to a movement. A performer may need
to analyse an error at a sensible break. “Trust the skill” cannot replace learning a missing skill or
listening to accurate feedback.
The distinction concerns timing and purpose. During practice, a coach can explain one correction.
During a familiar attempt, the performer may use one understood cue rather than rehearse a long
list of technical instructions. Afterwards, the action can be reviewed again.
Move from judgment to evidence
Use three parts: observation, possible explanation and next action. Keep the explanation open when
the evidence is limited. “My setup was shorter than usual; I may have rushed; I will use the agreed
setup cue next time” is more useful than “I always choke.”
A school example works the same way. “I left out the evidence for my claim” identifies something to
revise. “I am bad at every subject” does not. A realistic observation can support a clear correction
while preserving the fact that the work needs improvement.
The aim is not to remove every unhelpful thought. Notice when a thought pulls attention away, then
return to a task-relevant action. Review the pattern without grading yourself on whether your mind
felt perfectly quiet.

Learning goal: I can select a cue and anchor that fit a particular task.
Before you begin: A cue must connect to an action the performer understands and has
practised.
A cue is a reminder, not a complete lesson
A  cue word is a short word or phrase used to direct attention or support action. It works best when
the performer already understands its meaning. “Smooth” may remind Jordan of a practised release.
For someone who has not learned that action, the word may be too vague.
A useful cue is short enough to use in the available moment. “Change your feet, shoulders, hands
and timing” gives several competing instructions. During learning, those features may need separate
explanation. During a familiar attempt, select the cue most relevant to the identified task.
Instructional and motivational purposes
An   instructional cue directs technique, timing or relevant information. “See the target,” “steady
count” and “main evidence” can serve that purpose in different settings. The phrase should tell the
performer something useful about what to do.
A  motivational cue supports effort or commitment. “Keep going” or “commit to this phrase” can
serve that purpose. It should not pressure someone to ignore a real need for support. A more
intense phrase is not automatically a better one.
Classify a cue by the job it does, not only its wording. “Finish” could remind a musician to sustain a
final note or encourage a student to complete a familiar task. The explanation of its purpose makes
the distinction clear.
An anchor gives attention a return point
An   anchor is a chosen cue, sensation or action that helps the performer return to the task. A rim
target, an agreed musical count or a key word on a speaking card can be an anchor. The performer
should know when to use it and what comes next.
An anchor is not a lucky object that guarantees a result. It is also not necessarily a body check.
Sometimes the best return point is external information. Choose the anchor from the task rather than
adding a complicated routine because it sounds professional.
Plan the return
Use the sentence, “When I notice ___, I will return to ___, then ___.” The first part identifies a signal.
The second selects the anchor. The third connects attention to action. For example, “When I start
replaying the last error, I will look at the agreed entry mark, count in and begin the next phrase.”

The plan must allow flexibility. A usual visual anchor may not be available in a different room. Identify
an alternative that serves the same purpose. Test the cue during appropriate practice and review
whether it made the action clearer. Do not claim success merely because the phrase was repeated.
Worked example · fictional case
Two cues, one selection
Jordan considers “commit” and “see the rim target.” The first supports effort. The second
directs attention to specific external information. Jordan's stated problem is looking toward a
spectator before shooting, so the target cue is a better first match for this case.
The anchor is the chosen part of the rim, not the word alone. After finding it, Jordan follows
the practised setup. If Jordan has not learned the setup, the plan also needs instruction;
repeating the cue is not enough.

07 · Prepare your attention
Build a short sequence that connects preparation to the first action.
Learning goal: I can explain the purpose of each step in a before-performance routine.
Before you begin: Use an existing skill and a realistic amount of preparation time.
A routine organizes attention
A  preperformance routine is a planned sequence used before an action. It can include checking
the task, choosing a cue and preparing to begin. Its purpose is to make the next action clearer.
Completing a routine does not guarantee a successful outcome or require every nervous feeling to
disappear.
Keep the routine suited to the setting. A free throw provides a different pause from a moving team
play. A classroom presentation may allow a short check before speaking. A musical entry may need
immediate attention to a conductor. A routine that takes too long can interfere with the task it is
meant to support.
Begin with information and preparation
First identify what the performer must know. Where is the action taking place? What is the starting
cue? Is a rule or instruction unclear? Clarifying a task can be more useful than repeating a
motivational phrase over missing information.
Preparation also includes skills and materials. A presenter checks that the needed example is ready.
A player knows the agreed setup. A musician has practised the entry. Mental preparation works with
those resources; it does not replace them.
Phase 3 — The Focus
SPORTS PSYCHOLOGY · NEXT STEP
19
chunks.titleGuess: NEXT STEP · SPORTS PSYCHOLOGY Phase 3 — The Focus

chunks.text:
Give each step one job
A simple routine might have three parts: prepare, direct and begin. During preparation, the performer
checks the task and uses any familiar, comfortable settling action that is useful. During direction,
they choose the relevant cue. During beginning, they commit to the next practised action.
The names matter less than the purpose. Explain what each step directs attention toward. “Prepare”
is too broad without a detail. “Check the starting position and listen for the official's signal” is a task-
based instruction.
Use a complete fictional example
For a school presentation, the routine could be: check the graph and speaking order; recall the cue
“main relationship”; look toward the audience and begin the practised opening. The student may still
feel uncertain. The sequence provides an action without demanding a perfect feeling first.
For sport, a brief body check belongs only at a suitable pause. Do not add breathing drills during
swimming, active play or another task needing full attention. Describing a routine in writing is an
acceptable way to demonstrate its purpose in this preview.
Practise and revise the routine
A routine becomes more usable when its steps are understood and rehearsed. Try a hypothetical
walkthrough or an appropriately supervised practice. Observe whether the sequence fits the
available time and whether the final cue belongs to the task.
Record the routine separately from the result. One successful attempt does not prove that the
routine caused success. One mistake does not automatically make the routine useless. Use specific
observations to choose a sensible adjustment.
Worked example · fictional case
Prepare, direct, begin
Jordan's routine is: check the line and starting position; briefly release unnecessary shoulder
tension during the pause; find the rim target, use “smooth” and shoot. Each step has a
purpose. The final attention is on the target and familiar action, not on continually checking
feelings.
A teammate uses a different routine. That is not a problem if it fits their task. The assignment
asks Jordan to explain and adapt the chosen sequence, not prove there is one correct ritual
for everybody.

Use a disruption as a signal for a practical next response.
Learning goal: I can write an adaptable if–then plan that returns attention to useful
information.
Before you begin: A reset ends with the task; it is not an endless check of feelings.
Disruption is part of a changing task
A performer may hear an unexpected sound, miss an entry or receive a new instruction. A reset is a
brief response that helps them return to useful information. It does not erase the event. It creates a
bridge from what happened to what the next action needs.

chunks.text:
Start with a specific signal. “I am losing focus” is broad. “I keep replaying the last pass and have
stopped checking teammates” identifies the pattern more clearly. A useful signal can be noticed
without judging the whole person.
Use an if–then plan
An   if–then plan links a likely event to a response. “If the speaking order changes, then I will confirm
when I begin and use my opening cue” is practical. It names both a trigger and an action.
Avoid trying to predict every possible problem. Choose a likely disruption that fits the case. Explain
what the performer will do and what information they will attend to next. The response should be
brief enough for the setting and should not create a new safety problem.
Notice, adjust, return
One useful sequence is: notice the signal; make a proportionate adjustment during a suitable pause;
return to the next task cue. A familiar comfortable breath, release of unnecessary tension or brief
cue may be part of the adjustment. None is compulsory for every performer.
The goal is not to force calmness. Do not hold or force the breath, and stop a physical practice if
uncomfortable. A written walkthrough is always available. A performer in active play may need to
return directly to the relevant external information rather than begin an internal exercise.
When the first response does not fit
A plan should include a check. Did the instruction become clearer? Can the performer identify the
next cue? If not, another response may be needed. An unclear role may require a question. An
unsafe demand requires a change or appropriate support, not more self-talk.
A reset also differs from denying an error. Useful feedback can be reviewed at a suitable break. The
performer does not need to rehearse a whole technical analysis while the next attempt is starting.
Separate immediate refocusing from later learning.
Apply the sequence beyond sport
A musician who loses a count may listen for the next agreed entry cue. A student interrupted during
a presentation may pause, identify the last completed point and return to the main claim. A
recreational participant may ask for the instruction again. The wording changes, but the structure
remains connected to the demand.
Judge the plan by its fit, clarity and flexibility. A successful reset is not defined by the learner claiming
that every distracting thought disappeared.

Learning goal: I can propose a suitable variation and explain what evidence would guide an
adjustment.
Before you begin: Keep practice hypothetical or appropriately supervised; it is not a
punishment.
A plan should travel beyond one familiar setting
A focus plan may work in a quiet practice and need adjusting in another setting. The useful question
is not, “Can I force the same feeling everywhere?” It is, “Which information and actions still fit, and
which need to change?”
Flexible focus means adapting attention to the task while keeping a clear purpose. It does not
mean changing every cue after one mistake. Use evidence to decide which part of the plan needs
attention.
Change one condition deliberately
A hypothetical practice can vary the order of turns, the location of a visual cue or the amount of
preparation time. Choose a change related to a likely performance demand. State what remains the
same so the comparison is understandable.
For actual practice, use appropriate teacher or coach guidance. The variation should not involve
humiliation, unsafe distraction or exhaustion as a test of character. You can demonstrate the
reasoning through a written case or walkthrough without creating real pressure.
Observe the action before interpreting it
Record what the performer intended to notice and what they actually did. For example: “Jordan
looked toward the spectator after the missed shot and did not see the signal.” That observation is
more useful than “Jordan has bad focus.”
Then consider possible explanations. Was the signal clear? Had the drill changed? Was Jordan
replaying the error? A scenario may provide evidence for one explanation, but a single missed cue
does not establish every cause. A strong response identifies both the evidence and its limits.
Decide what to keep and what to adjust
Keep parts of the routine that still serve the task. Adjust the part affected by the changed condition. If
the usual visual anchor is hidden, choose another relevant anchor. If the next action is unclear,
clarify it rather than simply using the same cue more intensely.

Build review criteria
The levels describe evidence, not an automatic numeric grade.
Concept accuracy
Not yet shown: Key ideas are missing or incorrect.
Developing: Some relevant ideas appear, but distinctions need clarification.
Clear: Terms and distinctions are accurate in the stated case.
Thoughtful: Accurate distinctions are carried into a changed situation, with relevant limits.
Evidence and task fit
Not yet shown: The response does not use the case.
Developing: Some evidence is named, but the choice is weakly connected.
Clear: The selected response is supported by relevant case evidence.
Thoughtful: The response weighs relevant evidence and explains why an alternative fits less well.
Usable plan
Not yet shown: The plan is missing or cannot be followed.
Developing: Actions are present but vague or incomplete.
Clear: The sequence, cues and support are specific and workable.
Thoughtful: The plan remains concise while providing a sensible alternative when conditions change.

Glossary and sources
Attention
Selecting and using information for a task.
Concentration
Sustaining attention with information that matters.
Task-relevant
Useful for the action or decision currently needed.
Distraction
Information that competes with the current task.
Broad attention
Considering several relevant pieces of information.
Narrow attention
Selecting a specific cue.
Internal attention
Attention to thoughts or bodily sensations.
External attention
Attention to information in the surroundings.
Attention shift
A change in the information selected when the demand changes.
Nonjudgmental observation
A factual description without a verdict on personal worth.
Inner Game
Gallwey’s attributed coaching framework for discussing learned execution and interference.
Self 1 / Self 2
Model labels for commentary and learned execution, not brain structures.
Instructional cue
A brief reminder directing technique, timing or information.
Motivational cue
A brief reminder supporting effort or commitment.

Explain a proportionate adjustment and one uncertainty.
Decision cases
Case 1: A. The case supplies both the missed information and Jordan’s account. A broad-external
scan fits the passing decision. It would not be the same focus as a free throw.
Case 2: B. Keep the useful observation and correction. A global judgment does not guide the next
phrase. The response joins immediate refocusing with later practice.
Case 3: C. The task still needs an explanation of the graph. An available representation can support
it. Changing the anchor preserves the purpose without requiring the original display.
Transfer: identify a genuinely different situation, use its evidence to choose a response and explain
a relevant limit or adjustment.
Build field examples
Task and changing demand
Jordan needs a broad scan during open play and a precise target at the free-throw line.
Distractions and evidence
Replaying the miss is internal. Watching a spectator is external. Jordan’s account connects these to
the missed signal.
Useful focus now
Before the pass, broad-external attention includes available teammates and defenders.
Three moments and their triggers
Open play: scan teammates. Whistle: listen to the official. Free throw: find the chosen rim target.

chunks.text:
Cue examples and selection
“See the target” directs attention; “commit” supports effort. Jordan first needs the target cue.
Anchor and use
At the line, the rim target is the anchor. Jordan finds it before following the familiar setup.
Before-performance sequence
Prepare: check the starting position. Direct: find the target and use “smooth.” Begin: take the
practised shot.
Disruption and response
If the drill order changes and the role is unclear, ask where to begin, then identify the next cue.
Walkthrough with a changed demand
In a hypothetical practice, shorten the preparation pause. Keep the task the same and check
whether the essential target cue is still used.
Observation and adjustment
Hypothetically, Jordan looks away before the signal. Review the trigger for returning to the target
rather than label Jordan as unfocused.
Adapt to an unfamiliar task
The duet adds a partner’s timing cue. Plan a shared entry and return point rather than using the solo
routine unchanged.
Why attention must change
The passing decision needs several external cues, while a free throw uses a precise target. One
missed cue does not identify every possible cause.

chunks.text:
Written review
Review 1: Width concerns how much information is selected; direction concerns where it comes
from. A player scanning several teammates is broad-external. A brief check of one tension signal
during a pause is narrow-internal. The task determines whether either fits.
Review 2: Identify the purpose of the cue and choose an available alternative serving that purpose.
A printed keyword may replace a slide title. Explain the next action and check whether the new
anchor makes the explanation usable.
Review 3: Gallwey’s equation is an attributed coaching framework, not a measurement. Self 1 and
Self 2 are labels for discussing commentary and learned execution. The framework does not replace
skill learning, task knowledge or useful feedback.
Review 4: A useful revision replaces vague language with a specific task, cue, trigger or
observation. For example, “focus more” can become a named scan before a pass. Explain the
change and retain a limitation where the evidence does not establish a cause.
Checkpoint explanations
1: A.    The task changes from explaining to responding. Selection, sustained attention and a
purposeful shift work together.
2: B.    The issue is competing jobs in a specific moment. Learning-time analysis and later feedback
remain important.
3: C.    Several relevant cues in the surroundings make this broad-external attention.
4: D.    The selected information is one specific bodily sensation. That describes narrow-internal
attention.
5: A.    It organizes a discussion. It does not supply measured values or remove other influences on
performance.
6: B.    These are model labels, not anatomy, diagnoses or permanent learner categories.
